primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Loss of Gsα expression/function from GNAS abnormalities impairs receptor-coupled cAMP signaling in PTH target tissues. Renal PTH resistance reduces phosphaturia and calcitriol production, producing hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH; some forms also have Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
vignette: A child has short stature, a round face, brachydactyly with shortened metacarpals, and subcutaneous ossifications. Laboratory studies show hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and an elevated parathyroid hormone concentration. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is also mildly elevated.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractors: Autosomal dominant hypocalcemia due to activating CASR mutation
distractor_notes: Primary hypoparathyroidism produces low or inappropriately normal PTH, not elevated PTH indicating end-organ resistance.
Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism can produce Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features but lacks the PTH resistance and hypocalcemia/hyperphosphatemia shown here.
Activating CaSR variants cause hypocalcemia with suppressed or inappropriately low PTH and often hypercalciuria rather than an Albright phenotype with elevated PTH.
Vitamin D receptor resistance can cause hypocalcemia and rickets but does not explain the classic Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype and multihormone Gsα resistance.
key_expl: Pseudohypoparathyroidism is defined by end-organ resistance to PTH, producing hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH. GNAS inactivation can reduce Gsα-mediated cAMP signaling and, in classic forms, produce Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features such as brachydactyly, round facies, short stature, and ectopic ossification.
objective: Recognize pseudohypoparathyroidism as GNAS/Gsα-mediated hormone resistance causing hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH, and Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
